subject: Barøy et al. (2013)
object: Barøy et al. (2013) described 4 unrelated patients (2 females aged 15 and 6.5 years, 2 males aged 4 and 6.5 years; 3 Norwegian or Norwegian/English, 1 Lebanese, all of nonconsanguineous parents) with de novo 6p22.3 deletions including JARID2. All 4 had developmental delay with cognitive impairment ranging from borderline IQ to severe intellectual disability, gait disturbance with impaired balance and coordination, and similar facial dysmorphic features. These included prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, dark infraorbital circles, midface hypoplasia, bulbous nasal tip, full lips, marked Cupid's bow, and a prominent or pointed chin. Other features were clinodactyly of the fifth fingers and foot anomalies such as syndactyly of toes, along with seizures or seizure-suspected episodes in 2 patients, behavioral abnormalities in 3, autism spectrum disorder in 1, and an atrial septal defect in 1.

subject: Barøy et al. (2013)
object: Barøy et al. (2013) reported a 6.5-year-old Lebanese boy (Patient 4) of nonconsanguineous parents who had the smallest JARID2-containing deletion. He walked at 16 months and had language delay of 1.5 years at age 4 years 3 months, and his IQ was 74 (borderline) at 6.5 years. He had balance and coordination problems, poor finger opposition, and early-onset muscular hypotonia; neuromuscular and metabolic workups were normal, and cerebral MRI and EEG were normal. He had the characteristic facial features, strabismus, fifth-finger clinodactyly, syndactyly of toes 2-3, sandal gap, and broad halluces.

subject: Barøy et al. (2013)
object: In a cohort of about 3,600 patients ascertained for neurodevelopmental disorders, Barøy et al. (2013) used aCGH to identify de novo 6p22.3-p24.1 deletions in 5 patients. Deletions in 4 patients, ranging from 189 kb to 4.8 Mb, shared a smallest region of overlap (SRO I) of 189 kb that included JARID2 and DTNBP1. This region was defined by the 189-kb deletion in Patient 4, which removed exons 3 to 18 and the 3-prime UTR of JARID2 and exons 7 to 10 of DTNBP1. Parental testing showed that all deletions were de novo, and DGV contained only CNVs covering minor parts of the region.

subject: JARID2 189–241 kb deletion, including part of the genes JARID2 and DTNBP1 (exons 3–18 of JARID2)
Barøy et al. (2013)
object: Barøy et al. (2013) found that JARID2 expression in leukocyte RNA was significantly lower in the 4 patients with JARID2 deletion than in 8 healthy controls (p ≤ 0.01). They argued against DTNBP1 as the causal gene and concluded that JARID2, a transcriptional repressor and chromatin modifier acting in the PRC2 and Notch pathways, was likely the critical gene within SRO I.

subject: Barøy et al. (2013)
object: Barøy et al. (2013) reviewed 10 previously reported patients with deletions including JARID2. The characteristic facial features were not consistently reported in these patients, but inspection of photographs available for 7 of them confirmed a similar facial pattern. Four of the 10 had impaired balance, impaired coordination, and/or gait disturbance. The authors suggested that JARID2 haploinsufficiency may result in a clinically recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome and recommended sequencing JARID2 in similar patients without a deletion.

subject: Barøy et al. (2013)
object: Barøy et al. (2013) observed that Patient 5, a 17-year-old Norwegian girl with a de novo 116-kb deletion including GMPR and part of ATXN1 but not JARID2, had mild intellectual disability and behavioral abnormalities without the facial dysmorphism or gait disturbance. Patients 1 to 3, whose deletions included both JARID2 and ATXN1, had moderate to severe intellectual disability. The authors suggested that simultaneous deletion of both genes likely exacerbated the degree of intellectual disability.

subject: Zahir et al. (2016)
object: Zahir et al. (2016) had earlier found a CNV involving only exon 6 of the JARID2 gene, apparently de novo, in 7 patients with intellectual disability. JARID2 exon 6 encodes one of a series of repeated motifs, so the authors studied this variant in 2 cohorts and carried out a genotype-phenotype assessment. They concluded that the JARID2 exon 6 CNV is benign, with a high population frequency (more than 14%), although it could still have a contributory effect.

subject: JARID2 CNV involving only exon 6 of the JARID2 gene
Verberne et al. (2021)
object: Verberne et al. (2021) concluded that JARID2 haploinsufficiency causes a clinically distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome. Its features are developmental delay and/or intellectual disability and characteristic facial features.

subject: Verberne et al. (2021)
object: Verberne et al. (2021) reported 16 individuals from 15 families who had a deletion or single-nucleotide variant in JARID2. All had developmental delay and/or intellectual disability. They shared some clinical features, such as facial features, with individuals who have larger 6p22-p24 deletions that include JARID2.

subject: Verberne et al. (2021)
object: Verberne et al. (2021) used chromosome microarray analysis, exome sequencing and GeneMatcher to find deletions or single-nucleotide variants involving JARID2 in 16 individuals from 15 families. The authors suggested that several of the variants were likely to cause haploinsufficiency through nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

subject: Verberne et al. (2021)
object: Verberne et al. (2021) noted that 13 previously reported individuals with intellectual disability had de novo heterozygous 6p22-p24 deletions that removed all of JARID2. Every one of these deletions also removed at least one neighbouring gene, so it could not be determined whether JARID2 was the critical gene.

subject: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022)
object: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022) reported 7 individuals from 5 families with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants, which confirmed the gene-disease association. The cases highlighted palatal abnormalities and heart defects as part of the phenotype.

subject: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022)
object: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022) reported that JARID2 variants were inherited from mildly affected parents, which demonstrated variable expressivity of the disorder.

subject: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022)
object: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022) noted a high prevalence of intragenic JARID2 copy number variants among the patients and emphasized the importance of exon-level analysis.

subject: Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) described JARID2 haploinsufficiency as causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome. It is characterized by developmental delay, cognitive impairment ranging from borderline intellectual functioning to severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, autistic features, and behavior abnormalities. Dysmorphic facial features include a high anterior hairline, broad forehead, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, and full lips.

subject: Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) summarized 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants: 4 males and 4 females aged 5 to 36 years, 5 of whom had been reported previously. All 8 had developmental delay. Intellectual functioning ranged from normal (1 patient) through learning difficulties or borderline functioning to moderate ID. Other features were autistic features (4 of 8, 2 with an ASD diagnosis), behavior abnormalities (3), hypotonia (2), gait disturbance (2), and variable facial dysmorphism. Additional anomalies included submucous cleft palate with bifid uvula, cryptorchidism, an arachnoid cyst or posterior fossa cyst/mega cisterna magna, kyphoscoliosis, and cafe-au-lait macules.

subject: Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) reported 6 patients with deletions of at least one exon of JARID2 on chromosome 6p22.3, identified by microarray analysis or other methods. Five deletions were de novo. Patient 6 inherited her deletion from her mother (patient 7), who had learning difficulties.

subject: JARID2 deletion exons 6-18
Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) reported a 14-year-old boy (patient 4) with moderate ID, autism spectrum disorder, and behavior abnormalities. He carried a de novo heterozygous frameshift variant in JARID2, c.2866dupG (p.Glu956GlyfsTer72), which was classified as pathogenic.

subject: JARID2 c.15511546dup / c.2866dupg / p.E956G
Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) reported a 5-year-old boy (patient 5) with developmental delay, hypotonia, an arachnoid cyst, right cryptorchidism, and congenital torticollis. He carried a de novo heterozygous splice site variant in JARID2, c.2731+1G-C, which was classified as likely pathogenic.

subject: Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) analyzed peripheral blood DNA methylation (EPIC arrays) in 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants and 56 matched controls. They identified a 150-probe episignature that clearly separated patients from controls on hierarchical clustering and multidimensional scaling, and the signature held up in leave-one-out cross-validation. A support vector machine classifier gave all patients scores near 1 and gave controls and samples from 57 other disorders low scores, which the authors interpreted as full sensitivity and specificity.

subject: Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) tested 3 patients with JARID2 missense variants of uncertain significance against the episignature. Two unrelated patients (9 and 11) carried c.2363G-A (p.Arg788Gln); in patient 11 it was maternal, from an apparently unaffected mother. Patient 10 carried a de novo c.1930G-A (p.Glu644Lys) in the ARID domain. All 3 clustered with controls and had scores near zero. The authors noted this did not rule out pathogenicity but suggested the variants might be benign: patients 9 and 10 lacked the typical facial dysmorphism, and patient 11 had severe global spasticity and lack of myelination.

subject: Verberne et al. (2022)
object: Verberne et al. (2022) found no significant differentially methylated regions. Among the 150 episignature probes, they found 7 small regions with a consistent direction of effect. Two of these were annotated to genes previously linked to abnormal neurological development, NLGN2 and ADGRL2. Gene set enrichment did not identify consistent pathways.
